description: Phase 6cc — ambiguous-alias tiebreak. When >1 projection aliases share a name AND that name also matches a base column of the enclosing FROM, the base column wins and the query must compile. Pure-shadow duplicates (no matching base column) still raise COMPILE_AMBIGUOUS_ALIAS. Matches mainline SQLite semantics; unblocks random/groupby/slt_good_{8..12}.

cases.name: dup-alias-name-matches-base-col-group-by
cases.description: `SELECT col0 * col2 AS col0, col0 AS col0 ... GROUP BY col0, col2` — two projections aliased `col0` AND a base column `col0` exists. Mainline resolves GROUP BY `col0` to the base column. Canonical failing query from random/groupby/slt_good_8.test:55560.

program.sql: CREATE TABLE tab1 (col0 INTEGER, col1 INTEGER, col2 INTEGER);
SELECT col0 * col2 AS col0, col0 AS col0 FROM tab1 AS cor0 GROUP BY col0, col2 ORDER BY col0;

cases.name: dup-alias-name-matches-base-col-simple
cases.description: Simpler form — `SELECT + col0 AS col0, col0 AS col0 ... GROUP BY col0`. Alias count 2, name matches base column `col0`. Base column wins the GROUP BY tiebreak.

program.sql: CREATE TABLE tab1 (col0 INTEGER, col1 INTEGER);
INSERT INTO tab1 VALUES (22,1), (28,2), (82,3);
SELECT + col0 AS col0, col0 AS col0 FROM tab1 GROUP BY col0 ORDER BY col0;

cases.name: dup-alias-different-base-col-in-group-by
cases.description: Alias name = col0 (matches base col). Projection aliases shadow differently. GROUP BY col0 still resolves to base column, not to either alias.

program.sql: CREATE TABLE t (col0 INTEGER, col1 INTEGER);
SELECT col1 AS col0, col0 + 100 AS col0 FROM t GROUP BY col0 ORDER BY col0;
program._note: each row is its own group (col0 distinct), ORDER BY col0 picks base col -> 1,2,3,4 sort

cases.name: dup-alias-in-order-by-matches-base-col
cases.description: ORDER BY variant of the same rule — duplicate aliases with a base-column collision resolve ORDER BY to the base column.

program.sql: CREATE TABLE t (col0 INTEGER, col1 INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (3,30), (1,10), (2,20);
SELECT col0 AS col0, col1 * -1 AS col0 FROM t ORDER BY col0;

cases.name: dup-alias-in-having-matches-base-col
cases.description: HAVING variant — bare `col0` in HAVING with a duplicate alias whose name collides with base column. Base column wins the tiebreak so the HAVING filter uses the underlying value.

program.sql: CREATE TABLE t (col0 INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (10), (20), (30);
SELECT col0 + 100 AS col0, col0 * -1 AS col0 FROM t GROUP BY col0 HAVING col0 > 15 ORDER BY col0;

cases.name: dup-alias-pure-shadow-still-errors
cases.description: Regression guard — when NO base column matches the alias name AND the alias is duplicated AND a post-projection clause references it, AMBIGUOUS_ALIAS must still be raised. This is the pre-existing 6aj fixture semantic, unchanged.

program.sql: CREATE TABLE t (a INTEGER, b INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 10);
SELECT a AS x, b AS x FROM t ORDER BY x;

cases.name: single-alias-name-matches-base-col-order-by-unchanged
cases.description: Regression guard — single alias whose name shadows a base column still resolves the alias in ORDER BY (pre-6cc 6aj behavior untouched, alias count==1 path unchanged).

program.sql: CREATE TABLE t (a INTEGER, b INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 30), (2, 20), (3, 10);
SELECT b AS a FROM t ORDER BY a;

cases.name: dup-alias-qualified-col-never-ambiguous
cases.description: Qualified column `cor0.col0` is never treated as an alias, so duplicate aliases called `col0` do not poison qualified references in GROUP BY.

program.sql: CREATE TABLE tab1 (col0 INTEGER, col1 INTEGER, col2 INTEGER);
INSERT INTO tab1 VALUES (28,1,45), (22,2,8);
SELECT col0 * col2 AS col0, col0 AS col0 FROM tab1 AS cor0 GROUP BY cor0.col0, cor0.col2 ORDER BY cor0.col0;
